key_insight: Activation probes can detect misuse signals in large language models, but standard probe designs fail when inputs shift from short to long contexts; with architecture and training changes, probes can be made robust and production-ready for models like Gemini.
problem_solved: Existing activation probes do not generalize under the production distribution shift from short-context to long-context inputs, leading to unreliable misuse detection when deployed.
method: Design context-aware probe architectures (e.g., position-aware readouts, hierarchical pooling or attention over token-wise activations) to capture long-range signals.
Train with long-context augmentation and auxiliary/contrastive objectives that promote invariance across context lengths and improve calibration.
Adopt deployment strategies (sliding-window inference, lightweight ensembling, latency-aware layer selection) to maintain performance and throughput in production.
impact: Makes activation-based misuse detectors practical for production LMs by shrinking the short→long context generalization gap, improving reliability of safety monitoring for practitioners deploying models like Gemini.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: short-context probe success vs long-context probe failure (highlighting the generalization gap).
Architecture sketch showing the probe attached to model activations with position-aware pooling/attention layers.
Before/after bar or line chart illustrating reduced error or gap across context lengths after proposed changes.
Deployment flowchart showing sliding-window inference, ensembling, and latency vs accuracy trade-offs.
paper_authors: János Kramár, Joshua Engels, Zheng Wang, Bilal Chughtai, Rohin Shah
